stories.title: Producer Prices Flat in July as Goods Costs Fall
stories.excerpt: U.S. producer prices were unchanged in July as declining goods costs balanced out increases across services and construction, according to data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.  The Producer Price Index for final demand remained flat on a seasonally adjusted basis after edging down 0.1% in June and advancing 0.5% in May. Over the 12 months ending in July, unadjusted final demand prices increased 4.7%.  Excluding volatile food, energy, and trade services components, the core final demand index rose 0.4% in July following a modest 0.1% tick higher in June. On an annual basis, the index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services gained 4.7%.  Final-demand goods prices declined 0.7% in July after falling 1.4% in June. Energy prices dropped 3.1%, led by a 5.7% decrease in gasoline. Food prices declined 0.9%, while prices for goods excluding food and energy edged up 0.1%. Those declines were offset by a 0.2% increase in final-demand services and a 2.2% advance in construction prices.  Services excluding trade, transportation and warehousing  increased 0.6%. Portfolio-management prices surged 6.5%, while margins rose for several retail categories. Freight-trucking prices declined 1.8%, and trade-service margins slipped 0.1%.  The report may reduce the urgency for a September rate increase, but the strength in services and construction gives policymakers reason to remain cautious about declaring inflation contained.  The post Producer Prices Flat in July as Goods Costs Fall appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Producer Price Index flat July 2026; goods down 0.7%, construction up 2.2%
Core final demand +0.4% MoM, +4.7% YoY; energy fell 3.1%, services +0.2%
Construction prices accelerating despite broader deflation; sticky cost driver for developers
stories.summary: U.S. producer prices remained flat in July 2026 on a seasonally adjusted basis, with declining goods costs offsetting service and construction increases. Final-demand construction prices surged 2.2% in July, the steepest monthly gain. Core inflation excluding food and energy rose 0.4% monthly and 4.7% annually, signaling persistent pressure in services and construction materials despite broader goods deflation.
stories.impact: Construction cost inflation remains a headwind for multifamily development underwriting nationwide. While goods deflation improves material costs, construction services and labor costs are accelerating—tightening margins on new starts and raising hurdle rates. Developers should expect slower softening of hard costs than commodity prices alone suggest, pressuring feasibility in mid-to-low-yield markets.

stories.title: Walker Webcast: McKinsey’s Aditya Sanghvi Discusses Why and How Agentic AI Can Be Tailor-Made for Rental Housing
stories.excerpt: Artificial intelligence, particularly the agentic kind, could help rental housing owners and operators automate tasks, coordinate maintenance and improve resident retention. But getting there involves more than installing a new technology. “I would put out there that rental housing is perfect for AI,” said McKinsey & Co. senior partner Aditya Sanghvi, a leader of the firm’s global real estate practice. Sanghvi spoke at Walker & Dunlop’s recent annual convention in Sun Valley, Idaho, in a session broadcast Aug. 12 as a Walker Webcast. During the session, Sanghvi discussed why rental housing is well-suited to agentic AI, why adoption remains slow and what CEOs can do to get more value from the technology. Rental Housing Is Built for Agentic AI Unlike generative AI, which responds to human prompts, agentic AI is given a goal. The agent then plans and executes the tasks needed to achieve it. Multiple agents can also coordinate specialized processes. Sanghvi said that the technology perfectly matches property management, as the industry relies on numerous relatively simple tasks that become complicated when residents, property managers and vendors intersect. The result can be “dead zones,” the unfulfilled maintenance tickets, unanswered calls and missed follow-ups that can erode the resident experience. Agentic AI can help fill those gaps. In a maintenance situation, for example, one agent could triage requests, another could coordinate vendors, and another could handle scheduling. A separate agent could identify recurring problems and improve future decisions. Agentic AI could also improve lease conversions, renewals, collections and other repetitive processes. Over time, agents can learn from repeated decisions and become more effective. This doesn’t mean that humans are eliminated. “Humans are essential for the loop of every agent AI process,” Sanghvi said. Humans still outperform agents on many tasks. Also, agents can’t be held accountable.” Adoption Remains
bullets: McKinsey senior partner Sanghvi: agentic AI tailored for rental housing ops and maintenance
Technology automates resident tasks, coordinates maintenance, improves retention; adoption remains slow
AI well-suited to multifamily's fragmented task coordination; resolves 'dead zones' in service
stories.summary: McKinsey's Aditya Sanghvi discussed how agentic AI—which executes goals autonomously rather than responding to prompts—is uniquely suited to rental housing operations. The technology can automate maintenance coordination, resident communication, and vendor interactions. Adoption remains slow despite the fit, largely because implementation requires organizational change beyond software installation.
stories.impact: This signals emerging operational leverage for institutional multifamily operators willing to invest in automation infrastructure. Early adopters who deploy agentic AI for property management and resident retention will gain cost and satisfaction edges, especially critical as wage inflation pressures operating margins in tight labor markets. Expect increasing divergence between tech-forward and legacy operators on NOI.

stories.title: The Schedule C Trap: Why Your Biggest Deal This Year Might Be With the IRS
stories.excerpt: In real estate, we’re obsessed with the big numbers, what we “gross.” We talk about ‘GCI’ like it’s the only number that matters. We celebrate the $50 million year, the record-breaking penthouse sale, and the expansion into new markets (hello, California for SERHANT.!). But, after the 1099s are issued and the dust settles, a lot of agents realize that while they were busy selling the dream, they were living a tax reality that is — to put it bluntly — inefficient. The problem with ‘playing small’ Most agents start as “solopreneurs.” It’s you, your phone and a dream. You file as a sole proprietor because it’s easy. You run everything through a Schedule C because that’s what your first mentor told you to do. But here’s the truth: What worked for you when you were doing three deals a year is a financial impediment once you hit the big leagues. I call it the “Schedule C Trap.” When you’re a high-earner filing as a sole proprietor, you aren’t just paying income tax — you’re getting hammered by self-employment taxes on every single dollar you earn. We’re talking about a potential $10,000 to $30,000 “convenience fee” that you’re effectively handing to the government every year simply because you haven’t structured your business like a business. In 2026, the complexity has only ramped up. Between the shifting SALT cap limits and the new surcharges on high-income filers in hubs like New York, the “wait and see” approach to accounting is no longer a viable strategy — it’s a massive liability. Beyond the shoe box We’ve all been there: the April 14th panic. You’re digging through glove boxes for gas receipts, charity donation receipts, scrolling through Venmo history to remember if that “lunch meeting” was for a client or a cousin, and praying your accountant doesn’t fire you. bullets: Real estate professionals face self-employment tax inefficiency under Schedule C sole proprietor filing

Article about broker comp optimization; no direct bearing on multifamily development economics
stories.summary: A column warns real estate agents and brokers that filing as sole proprietors under Schedule C creates unnecessary self-employment tax exposure as income scales. Professionals earning $50 million or more annually incur significant tax drag that could be eliminated through entity restructuring (LLC, S-Corp, C-Corp). The piece argues that strategies optimal at three deals per year become liabilities at scale.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. This applies to brokerage and agent economics, not capital formation or development feasibility. However, indirectly, high-net-worth individuals who optimize personal tax structures may have more capital available for real estate co-investments or equity raises—a marginal boost to capital pools for development sponsors.

stories.title: Luxury Condo Sales in Manhattan Rise Post-Pied-à-Terre Rollout
stories.excerpt: The luxury pied-à-terre is alive and well, despite any efforts to stifle — or excessively tax — it. While the second week of August saw a Staten Island Supreme Court judge block the rollout of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax — a controversial surcharge on second homes worth more than $5 million — the first week of the month saw a year-over-year rise in such sales. From Aug. 1 to Aug. 7, there were 16 contracts signed above $5 million, a 7 percent year-over-year increase when compared to the same week in 2025, according to data from Corcoran Sunshine shared exclusively with Commercial Observer. In addition, since the passage of the tax some 16 weeks ago, sales of condos, co-ops and townhomes worth more than $5 million are up 1 percent from those 16 weeks last year, and up 3 percent versus the five-year average, the data shows. Overall, Manhattan saw 302 sales over $5 million from April 18 to Aug. 7, versus 268 sales tracked from Jan. 31 to April 17. For that same time period of April to August, sales of homes worth between $5 million and $15 million are up 2 percent year-over-year, while sales of homes worth between $15 million and $25 million are up 8 percent. However, homes valued at higher prices, like $25 million and more, are down 20 percent year-over-year — but that doesn’t mean they aren’t selling. The largest contract signed during the week of Aug. 1 to Aug. 7 was a full-floor residence at 1122 Madison Avenue worth $40.5 million. Sentiment around Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax has certainly been mixed since the legislature was passed at the end of May, especially after the mayor posted a controversial video that called out Citadel CEO Ken Griffin by name over his $238 million Manhattan penthouse and caused some to speculate that Griffin might abandon the planned tower Citadel was building in Midtown and focus instead on Florida. stories.summary: A Staten Island judge blocked Mayor Zohran Mamdani's proposed pied-à-terre tax on second homes worth over $5 million in early August 2026. Despite the tax's passage 16 weeks prior, luxury condo sales above $5 million rose 1% versus the same period last year, and 7% in the first week of August. Sales of homes between $5 million and $15 million gained 2% year-over-year.
stories.impact: Removal of pied-à-terre tax uncertainty removes a cloud over Manhattan luxury condo development economics and investor confidence. While the article focuses on resale/secondary market, the injunction signals sustained demand from international and domestic high-net-worth buyers, validating luxury rental conversion and new-build condo feasibility in Manhattan's core submarkets. No immediate pressure on rental demand, but supports valuation of luxury rental comps.

stories.title: AV Management Nabs SoHo Mixed-Use for $43M
stories.excerpt: Cushman & Wakefield arranged the sale of 73-75 Sullivan St., a newly constructed mixed-use property totaling 32,957 square feet and comprising 11 residential units and a ground-floor commercial space anchored by The Montessori School. The final sale price was $43,333,000. A Cushman & Wakefield team of Dylan Walsh, Niko Nicolaou, Ryan Dowd and Andrew Berry represented the seller, 73-75 Sullivan Partners-1, LLC, and procured the buyer, AV Management. “This sale underscores the continued demand for high-quality multifamily assets in core Manhattan neighborhoods,” said Walsh. “The property’s fully free-market status and prime SoHo location generated strong investor interest, reflecting the enduring strength of New York’s multifamily investment market.” The property benefits from immediate access to multiple subway lines, including the C, E, 1 and 6 trains. Residents and commercial tenants enjoy proximity to world-class retail, dining and cultural destinations, as well as convenient access to parks, fitness centers and grocery stores, Cushman & Wakefield said. The transaction reflects continued investor demand for high-quality multifamily in core Manhattan neighborhoods.
stories.impact: This small-scale, newly built Manhattan multifamily sale at ~$3.94M per unit validates that core SoHo infill development remains highly competitive and commands premium pricing. The ability to blend residential with institutional ground-floor tenancy (school) demonstrates mixed-use optionality for Manhattan developers. For TCR, this signals continued investment velocity in tight-supply, prime-location submarkets; development feasibility remains strong if land basis supports underwriting.

stories.title: U.S. Multifamily Gains Momentum in Q2 2026 as Absorption Surges
stories.excerpt: The U.S. multifamily market gained momentum in the second quarter of 2026 as apartment demand accelerated and new construction continued to moderate, CBRE said Wednesday. Net absorption of 167,500 units nearly doubled the Q1 tally, while the national multifamily vacancy rate declined by 50 basis points quarter-over quarter to 4.3%, below its long-term average of approximately 5.0%. New supply growth continued to ease, with 77,700 units delivered in Q2 2026, a 14% decrease from a year earlier. Average monthly rent rose 0.5% year-over-year and 1.5% quarter-over-quarter to $2,257 in Q2 2026. Multifamily investment volume totaled $34.9 billion in Q2 2026, down 2.7% from a year earlier. Even so, the multifamily sector remained the largest property sector for commercial real estate investment during the quarter, accounting for 27% of total volume. “The supply wave in the U.S. multifamily sector is cresting, with deliveries down 14% year-over-year and absorption nearly doubling quarter-over-quarter,” said Kelli Carhart, head of multifamily capital markets for CBRE. “Multifamily is positioned for its strongest rent recovery since 2022.” Where the apartment industry connects. stories.summary: The U.S. multifamily market accelerated in Q2 2026 with net absorption of 167,500 units nearly doubling Q1 levels, while the national vacancy rate compressed 50 basis points to 4.3%, below the 5% long-term average. New supply continued to ease, with deliveries down 14% year-over-year to 77,700 units. Average rents rose 1.5% quarter-over-quarter to $2,257, and multifamily investment volume totaled $34.9 billion, remaining the largest CRE sector at 27% of total.
stories.impact: The supply wave is cresting nationally—this is the inflection point where years of overbuilding resolve into a tight market and rent growth accelerates. For TCR developers, this signals a window to fast-track deliveries in Q3–Q4 2026 to capture pent-up demand before competitor leasing ramps; cap rates likely to compress as absorption/occupancy improve. Focus on near-term (18–24 month) delivery windows and markets with above-average absorption to maximize rent recovery tailwinds.

stories.title: TikTok Tells U.S. Employees to Return to Office 5 Days a Week
stories.excerpt: TikTok’s work-from-home era is scrolling to an end. The ByteDance-owned social media platform has instructed its U.S. employees to return to the office five days a week, sources told Business Insider. The change impacts the company’s hybrid employees that are currently allowed to work from home at least one day per week. TikTok alerted employees across several large divisions in December to expect a full office return in 2026, according to Insider, although certain teams, like TikTok’s e-commerce division, resumed five-day office attendance more than a year ago. TikTok employs thousands of U.S. employees across dozens of metro office locations, including its Culver City headquarters in Greater Los Angeles, and a seven-floor spread at the Durst Organization’s One Five One tower in Manhattan’s Times Square. TikTok earlier this month announced the closure of its 250-person Nashville office, however, just two years since opening. Return-to-office policies have been gaining ground across the country and across industries this year, Commercial Observer previously reported. U.S. office visits rose 6 percent year-over-year in the first half of 2026, and achieved the narrowest first-half gap from pre-pandemic levels thus far. The return-to-office wave has continued to buoy post-pandemic office leasing in cities like New York, where returning demand has driven rents to record highs this year. TikTok’s move to reign in work-from-home follows similar moves by its competitors Instagram and Amazon. Amazon’s office workers returned for five-day work weeks nearly two years ago, while other large technology companies, like YouTube and Patreon, have maintained their hybrid schedules. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: TikTok mandates 5-day office return for U.S. hybrid employees; e-commerce division already back full-time

stories.summary: TikTok's leadership directed U.S. hybrid employees to return to the office five days per week starting in 2026, reversing pandemic-era flexibility. The mandate impacts thousands of employees across multiple metro locations, including the company's Culver City, California headquarters and its seven-floor presence at One Five One in Manhattan's Times Square. TikTok recently closed its Nashville office of 250 employees after just two years.
stories.impact: TikTok's RTO mandate signals renewed corporate commitment to office density in Los Angeles and Manhattan, improving near-term office market fundamentals and occupier retention in prime tech corridors. However, the Nashville closure suggests geographic consolidation away from secondary markets—a headwind for multifamily demand outside primary metros. For TCR, focus development in LA (Culver City/West LA), Manhattan, and other RTO-leading tech hubs; avoid speculative multifamily in secondary markets losing tech job clusters.

stories.title: Blackstone Snaps Up Ken Griffin’s 125 Worth Avenue in Palm Beach for $86M
stories.excerpt: Billionaire Ken Griffin just parted ways with his last remaining retail property on Worth Avenue in Palm Beach, Fla., Commercial Observer has learned. Blackstone Real Estate has agreed to acquire the three-story office and retail building at 125 Worth Avenue, owned by Griffin since 2023, for $86 million in an all-cash deal, sources familiar with the trade said. Griffin previously bought the roughly 50,000-square-foot property from Dreyfuss Management and Frisbie Group for $83 million in 2023. “High-street retail continues to experience strong fundamentals, and Palm Beach represents one of the highest performing luxury retail markets in North America,” Elena Clarfield, principal at Blackstone Real Estate, told Commercial Observer. Indeed, as a retail corridor, the world famous Worth Avenue enjoys extreme scarcity when it comes to supply, coupled with soaring demand from a deluge of high-income residents into Palm Beach. Limited supply has also driven up property valuations in the prestigious area, evidenced by Acadia Realty Trust’s March 2026 acquisition of 225 Worth Avenue, leased to Gucci, for $43 million, or more than $4,329 per square foot. Blackstone declined to comment further but sources said the firm now intends to renovate the property, upgrading both the retail and office components to better align them with the continued evolution of Worth Avenue, a high-scale shopping district that’s home to several luxury tenants including Chanel, Louis Vuitton, Ferragamo and Van Cleef & Arpels. Representatives for Griffin could not immediately be reached for comment. The transaction represents Griffin’s second disposition on Worth Avenue in under a year. Last November, the billionaire sold his 48,578-square-foot property at 151 Worth Avenue to the family of GoldenTree Asset Management financier Steven Tananbaum, Commercial Observer reported at the time. Blackstone highlighted strong fundamentals in high-street luxury retail, driven by scarcity and soaring demand from affluent residents relocating to Palm Beach.
stories.impact: This transaction reflects institutional validation of Palm Beach as a ultra-prime, supply-constrained luxury market with resilient high-income demographic tailwinds. While focused on retail, it signals broader wealth migration into South Florida and confirms the robustness of multifamily demand and rents in Palm Beach, Miami Beach, and greater South Florida. For TCR, this reinforces South Florida as a prime market for upscale rental development; luxury multifamily in Palm Beach/Miami submarkets will benefit from demographic and capital inflows supporting rents.

stories.title: Fund Administrator Hanover Park Inks 19K-SF Deal at 387 Park Avenue South
stories.excerpt: An artificial intelligence-driven fund administrator is moving its headquarters to TF Cornerstone’s 387 Park Avenue South, Commercial Observer has learned. Hanover Park signed a 19,269-square-foot lease on the entire 10th floor of the NoMad property, marking its fifth office move in two years, according to CEO Chris Hladczuk. The firm’s most recent office address is listed on its website as 115 East 23rd Street. TF Cornerstone did not immediately provide the asking rent or the length of the lease, but the average asking rent for office space in Midtown South was $85.73 per square foot in the second quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “Existing tenants are choosing to expand here and new companies are choosing to locate here,” Joe Lanzilotta, director of commercial asset management at TF Cornerstone, said in a statement. “The property continues to outperform the market as a destination for growing businesses.” It is unclear who represented the tenant in the transaction, but Cushman & Wakefield’s Ethan Silverstein handled negotiations on behalf of the landlord in the deal signed in July. It’s unclear who represented the tenant. “The combination of TF Cornerstone’s long-term investment, highly efficient 20,000-square-foot floor plates and premier NoMad location continues to resonate with tenants,” Silverstein said in a statement. “The recent leasing activity demonstrates that companies are prioritizing best-in-class buildings, and with one full floor becoming available this fall, the property remains well positioned to meet continued demand.” Other recent deals in the 230,000-square-foot building at the corner of Park Avenue South and East 27th Street include a lease for marketing firm PMG Worldwide, which expanded from the second to third floor in May and brought its total footprint there to 38,744 square feet, according to TF Cornerstone. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Hanover Park (AI-driven fund administrator) leases 19.3K SF floor at 387 Park Ave South, Manhattan

stories.summary: Hanover Park, an AI-driven fund administrator, signed a 19,269-square-foot lease on the entire 10th floor of TF Cornerstone's 387 Park Avenue South in Manhattan's NoMad submarket. The transaction marks the company's fifth office relocation in two years. Midtown South average asking rent in Q2 2026 was $85.73 per square foot, and TF Cornerstone's property continues to outperform the broader market.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily. However, sustained Class A office leasing in Midtown South/NoMad by growing fintech and AI firms signals job density and wage earner concentration in Manhattan—positive for rental demand nearby. The frequency of Hanover Park's moves suggests rapid hiring and growth; employee in-migration supports rental demand in lower Manhattan and nearby multifamily submarkets. Indirect validation of Manhattan rental market strength in tech-adjacent employment nodes.
